analysis.one_liner: Restores an expired tax on oil and chemical companies to fund toxic waste site cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors after Senator Booker introduced it in January 2020.
analysis.plain_summary: From 1980 to 1995, companies that made oil and toxic chemicals paid an excise tax that filled the Superfund, the federal program that cleans up the country's worst abandoned hazardous waste sites. That tax expired in 1995, and since then general taxpayer money has had to cover cleanups. This bill would bring the tax back at a higher rate, adjust it for inflation going forward, expand it to cover oil from tar sands and oil shale, and let the Superfund spend its money without needing a new vote of Congress every year.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near toxic waste sites gain faster, better-funded cleanups, since the bill makes roughly $2-3 billion a year of industry money available to the Superfund without yearly congressional approval. Ordinary taxpayers also gain, because cleanup costs shift back from the general treasury to the oil and chemical companies that created the contamination. The Congressional Budget Office has previously estimated similar reinstatements at billions per year, though this bill's own estimate is not in the provided sources, so the specific figure here rests on the tax rates in the bill text rather than a scored cost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near toxic waste sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, which has not applied since 1995, at 15.8 cents per barrel of crude oil, up from the old 9.7 cents, with automatic inflation adjustments after 2019.
Reinstates and raises the excise tax on 42 listed hazardous chemicals, ranging from about 63 cents to $11.78 per ton depending on the chemical, also adjusted for inflation.
Expands the definition of taxable crude oil to include oil derived from tar sands and oil shale, so those producers pay the same financing rate as conventional crude.
Changes the law so money in the Superfund can be spent on cleanups without further annual appropriations, removing the yearly congressional vote that currently gates spending from the fund.

analysis.who_pays: Crude oil producers, refiners, and importers pay 15.8 cents per barrel (plus inflation adjustments), and chemical manufacturers pay a per-ton tax on listed hazardous chemicals. Some portion of these excise taxes can be passed through to consumers in fuel and product prices, but the tax is levied on the producers at the point of manufacture or entry, and its purpose is to make the industries whose products created toxic sites fund the cleanup.

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on oil and chemicals are ultimately business costs that producers can pass along in fuel and product prices, so a share of the burden could land on consumers rather than company profits.

The bill raises rates substantially above the historical level (from 9.7 to 15.8 cents per barrel) rather than simply restoring the old tax, and it sweeps in tar sands and oil shale production, which affected industries would characterize as a new tax rather than a restoration.
Letting the Superfund spend without annual appropriations reduces congressional oversight of how cleanup dollars are used, a trade-off a supporter would have to defend.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is well defined: a modest per-barrel and per-ton tax on oil and chemical production funds cleanup of hazardous waste sites that otherwise falls on general taxpayers. The main design risk is cost pass-through to consumers and the loss of annual appropriations oversight, both of which are real but smaller than the direct benefit of shifting cleanup costs back to the industries tied to the pollution. The bill is simple and targeted, though it never advanced far enough for any committee analysis of its effects.

outcome.mechanism: Booker introduced it on January 8, 2020, and the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Restoration Act of 2020 in the Senate on January 8, 2020.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was taken.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its entire life.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without the Finance Committee acting on the bill, so it died at the end of the two-year session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Crude oil and chemical producers are better off: the tax that would have raised their costs by roughly $2-3 billion a year was never enacted, and hazardous site cleanup costs continue to fall on general taxpayers. Communities near toxic sites gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the Superfund excise taxes; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 8, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for committee action during 2020

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no Republican and no other Democrat ever put their name on it, and it never reached a vote where party splits could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have charged them 15.8 cents per barrel, adjusted for inflation, and extended the tax to tar sands and oil shale output. Their interest in blocking it runs against the public's interest in funded toxic site cleanups.

The bill reinstates a per-ton excise tax on 42 hazardous chemicals including benzene, mercury, arsenic, and lead compounds, many of which are tied to Superfund contamination. They would have paid the tax that now falls on taxpayers instead.

industries.industry: Oil shale and tar sands producers
industries.note: The bill rewrites the definition of crude oil to explicitly cover bitumen, tar sands, and kerogen-bearing sources, bringing these producers under the Superfund tax for the first time in that form.
A funded Superfund with appropriations-free spending would mean more and steadier government-funded cleanup work. Their interest in funded cleanups runs alongside the public's.
